Operators: the [**Kubernetes** gaps](/?date=2026-10-27&category=research#item-hn-49977400) (no official **Helm** chart, root-at-init image) remain the highest-impact deployment finding, and the [~**23,000**-open-PR backlog](/?date=2026-10-27&category=research#item-hn-49424643) discussion continues. top_items.title: Hermes llama.cpp: One-Click Local Models in Hermes Agent
top_items.content:
Hermes llama.cpp support means you can now run AI models fully on your own computer from inside Hermes Agent, with no account, no API key and no internet connection once the model is downloaded. Hermes installs and maintains llama.cpp for you, picks the right engine for your hardware, and rates every model in its catalog against your GPU and RAM so you know what will actually run. In this guide I cover how the one-click setup works, how Hermes picks a model, the settings worth knowing and when local models make sense. Watch the video below, then try it.

Key takeaways

- Hermes now installs and maintains llama.cpp with the right engine: CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan or ROCm.

- Start from Settings → Providers → Local Models or `hermes model` → Local models.

- Models are colour-rated: green fits your GPU, amber uses system RAM, red is too big.

- Want local models set up properly? Claim a free strategy session.

## What is llama.cpp, and why does it matter for Hermes?

llama.cpp is the open-source engine that runs AI models on ordinary computers. It’s what a lot of local AI tools use under the hood. Until now, using it with Hermes meant installing it yourself, choosing the right build for your graphics card, downloading a model file and pointing Hermes at the server.

According to Hermes’ Local Models docs, Hermes now does all of that for you. It installs and maintains llama.cpp with the right engine for your machine, rates every catalog model against your GPU and memory, and starts and stops the model server along with Hermes.

The headline benefit is privacy and independence: the model runs on your machine, so there’s no account, no API key and no network needed after the download.

## How to set up local models in Hermes

There are two ways in, and both work on Windows, macOS and Linux:

- Hermes Desktop: Settings → Providers → Local Models.

- The terminal: run `hermes model` and choose Local models.

From there it’s three steps: Install runtime, Download a model, then Use it. Downloads can pause and resume, so a big model on a slow connection isn’t a problem.

Hermes picks the engine for you. Every backend runs the same llama.cpp build (b11370 at the time of writing). On Linux, NVIDIA cards get CUDA, while AMD and Intel cards get Vulkan. macOS uses Metal, and every platform has a CPU fallback. If you want to force a backend, the config has a `local_runtime.backend` setting that accepts `auto`, `cuda`, `metal`, `vulkan`, `hip` or `cpu`.

## How Hermes picks a model for your machine

This is the part I like most. Instead of guessing which model your computer can handle, Hermes rates every model in its catalog against your hardware and colour-codes it:

Colour
What it means

Green
Fits fully in your GPU memory — the fastest option

Amber
Spills into system RAM — it runs, but slower

Red
Too big for this machine

Hermes recommends the highest-quality model that fits fully in GPU memory at a predicted 20 tokens per second or more. It never goes below 4-bit quantisation, and every recommended model gets at least 64K of context, which grows as needed.

The catalog includes models such as Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.8 Flash Next, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B and DeepSeek V4 Flash. You’re not limited to the list: “Find more models” searches any GGUF model on Hugging Face, and “Add model file” loads a.gguf you already have on disk.

Want the right local model picked and tuned for your hardware? Claim your free strategy session →

Claim Your Free SEO Strategy Session →

## Settings worth knowing

- Idle unload. Models unload after 15 minutes of no use, so they don’t hold your GPU memory all day.

- Engine updates. When a new llama.cpp build is ready, Hermes shows an “Update now” prompt.

- Check your resources. In Hermes Desktop, right-click the status bar and choose System resources to see GPU and RAM use.

- Fallback. If your main provider fails, Hermes can fall back to the desktop-managed local model.

If you already run your own llama-server, Hermes detects it too. By default it checks port 8080; to check other ports, add them under `local_runtime.detect_ports`. A server you started yourself shows up in `/model`.

```
local_runtime:
  enabled: false
  backend: auto   # auto|cuda|metal|vulkan|hip|cpu
  detect_ports: [8081]
```

You can also point Hermes at a llama.cpp server directly with the `llamacpp` provider (aliases `llama.cpp` and `llama-cpp`):

```
providers:
  llamacpp:
    base_url: http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1
    model: my-model
```

LM Studio users get their own provider profile as well, and the Ollama model picker no longer flickers.

## System requirements

Platform
Supported engines

Windows
CUDA, Vulkan (x64) or CPU

Linux
CUDA (CUDA 13 driver), Vulkan or CPU

macOS
Metal or CPU

You don’t need a top-end graphics card to try it. The colour ratings tell you honestly what your machine can run, and a smaller green model will usually feel better than a bigger amber one.

## When local models make sense (and when they don’t)

Local models are a great fit when:

- You handle private or client data that you don’t want leaving your machine.

- You want Hermes to keep working offline or on a poor connection.

- You run lots of simple, repetitive jobs — sorting, summarising, tagging — where a small fast model is enough.

They’re a weaker fit for the hardest coding and reasoning work, where the biggest hosted models are still ahead. The smart setup is both: a local model for everyday and private work, and a hosted model for the heavy lifting. Hermes’ fallback option makes that easy.

If you want to compare specific local models I’ve tested, see my guides to the Flint local coding model, Spark X2 6.4B and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt in Hermes.

## My verdict on Hermes llama.cpp

Running models locally used to be a weekend project. Hermes turns it into a few clicks: it installs the engine, tells you what fits, downloads the model and manages the server. If you’ve wanted a private, offline agent, Hermes llama.cpp support is the easiest way I’ve seen to get one.

I’m Julian Goldie — founder of Goldie Agency and the AI Profit Boardroom. I test new AI agents almost every day for 432K+ YouTube subscribers and run Hermes, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Claude and Codex side by side in my own Agent OS. Claim your free strategy session or join the AI Profit Boardroom.

### Does Hermes Agent support llama.cpp?

Yes. Hermes installs and maintains llama.cpp for you from Settings, Providers, Local Models or hermes model, and you can also point it at your own llama-server with the llamacpp provider.

### Do I need an API key to run local models in Hermes?

No. Local models run fully on your machine with no account, no API key and no network once the model is downloaded.

### Which GPUs work with Hermes local models?

NVIDIA cards use CUDA, AMD and Intel cards use Vulkan on Linux, Macs use Metal, and every platform can fall back to CPU.

### How does Hermes choose which local model to recommend?

It rates each model against your GPU and RAM and recommends the highest-quality one that fits fully in GPU memory at a predicted 20 tokens per second or more, never below 4-bit.

### Can I use my own GGUF model in Hermes?

Yes. Use Find more models to search GGUF models on Hugging Face, or Add model file to load a.gguf file you already have.

top_items.title: Hermes Notion: 3 Ways to Connect Hermes Agent to Notion (2026)
top_items.content:
Hermes Notion is now one of the easiest setups in Hermes Agent, because version 0.22 gives you three official ways to plug Hermes into your Notion workspace. You can use the new Connectors feature, add Notion’s hosted MCP server from the built-in catalog, or use the notion skill that ships with Hermes. Each one lets Hermes read your pages, write new ones and work with your databases. In this guide I explain what each option does, which one to pick, and the Notion workflows I’d set up first. Watch the video below, then follow the steps.

Key takeaways

- Three ways in: Connectors (v0.22), the Notion MCP server, or the bundled notion skill.

- Connectors: ask Hermes for Notion, sign in once in the browser, and the tools work in the same turn.

- The skill uses a Notion integration key ( `NOTION_API_KEY`) and Notion’s official `ntn` CLI.

- Want Notion and Hermes set up for your team? Claim a free strategy session.

## What Hermes Notion actually means

Hermes Agent is the open-source AI agent from Nous Research. On its own it can chat, run commands, browse and remember things. Connecting it to Notion means Hermes can also work inside the place where many teams keep their notes, docs, project trackers and wikis.

Once it’s connected, you can ask Hermes things like “summarise this week’s meeting notes”, “turn this chat into a Notion page” or “add these leads to my CRM database”, and it does the work in Notion for you instead of handing you text to copy and paste.

Since Hermes Agent v0.22.0 (14 October 2026) there are three supported ways to do this. They overlap, so the trick is picking the one that matches how you work:

- Connectors — the newest and simplest. Hosted apps, a browser sign-in, no keys to copy.

- The Notion MCP server — Notion’s own hosted MCP endpoint, added from Hermes’ MCP catalog.

- The bundled notion skill — a skill that teaches Hermes to use the Notion API and Notion’s `ntn` command-line tool with your own integration key.

## Option 1: Connect Notion with Hermes Connectors

Connectors arrived in v0.22. In Nous’ words, they let the agent act in hosted apps such as Linear and Notion through the Nous tool gateway. The flow is short: you ask Hermes for the app, sign in once in your browser, and the Notion tools are usable in the same turn.

You don’t need a Nous account to start. The first time Hermes manages a connection (or you connect from the Desktop app’s Connectors page) it creates a free Nous identity for you. That identity is only used for connectors and managed tools.

There are three places to manage connections:

- Hermes Desktop: the Connectors page lists hosted apps and MCP servers together. It replaces the old MCP tab.

- The TUI: type `/connectors`. The same setup card shows up in the TUI and the CLI.

- The CLI: `hermes connectors list`, `hermes connectors connect notion`, and `hermes connectors disconnect notion`.

Connectors also support several named accounts per app, which is handy if you keep a work Notion and a personal one. Add a second account with `hermes connectors connect notion --alias home`. Names can be 1–32 characters using lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. There’s no default account — the tools take a `connector_alias`, so Hermes always knows which workspace it’s writing to. Reconnecting never deletes anything; the old account is kept as retired, and only you can remove accounts.

One more useful detail: connector tools can send local files as attachments and save the files they return, so Hermes can attach a report it made on your machine to a Notion page.

## Option 2: Add the Notion MCP server

Hermes has a built-in MCP catalog of hosted remote servers, including Atlassian, Sentry, Notion, Stripe, Vercel and Supabase. In Hermes Desktop these show up as suggestion pills in the composer, so you can add one in a click.

Notion’s hosted MCP endpoint is `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`. You can also manage servers from the terminal: `hermes mcp catalog` shows what’s available, `hermes mcp install <name>` adds one, and `hermes mcp login <server>` runs the sign-in for servers that use OAuth.

Why pick MCP over Connectors? If you already run other MCP servers, or you want to choose exactly which tools Hermes can call, MCP gives you that control in one place. If you just want Notion working with the least effort, Connectors is the shorter path.

Want Hermes writing to your Notion every day without babysitting it? Claim your free strategy session →

Claim Your Free SEO Strategy Session →

## Option 3: Use the bundled notion skill

Hermes also ships with a notion skill (version 2.0.0, MIT licence) that works on Linux, macOS and Windows. It describes itself as “Notion API + ntn CLI” and covers pages, databases, markdown and Workers.

This route uses your own Notion integration key instead of a hosted sign-in:

- Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations. The key starts with `ntn_` or `secret_`.

- Save it as `NOTION_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env`.

- Share your pages with the integration using the page menu (…) → Connect to. If you skip this, the API returns 404 and Hermes can’t see the page.

On macOS and Linux the skill can also use `ntn`, Notion’s official CLI. Install it with `npm install --global ntn` (Node 22 or later) or Notion’s install script, then set `NOTION_API_TOKEN=$NOTION_API_KEY` and `NOTION_KEYRING=0` so it picks up the same key. On Windows the skill uses plain HTTP calls with curl instead.

One thing that trips people up: in the current Notion API (version `2025-09-03`), databases are called data sources. If Hermes talks about querying a data source, it means your database.

## Which Hermes Notion option should you pick?

Option
Setup
Best for

Connectors
Ask Hermes or use the Connectors page, sign in once
Most people — fastest, several accounts, no keys

Notion MCP server
Add from the MCP catalog, OAuth sign-in
People already running MCP servers who want tool-level control

notion skill
Integration key in ~/.hermes/.env, share pages
Self-hosters who want their own key and the ntn CLI

My advice: start with Connectors. If you later want finer control, add the MCP server. Use the skill when you’d rather not route through the Nous gateway, or you want the extra commands `ntn` gives you, such as uploading files with `ntn files create`.

## 5 Hermes Notion workflows worth setting up

Connecting is the easy part. The value comes from giving Hermes regular jobs. These are the ones I’d start with:

- Meeting notes to action items. Ask Hermes to read a meeting page as markdown, pull out the tasks and add them to your tasks database with owners and due dates.

- Chat to page. When a conversation with Hermes produces something useful — a plan, a brief, an SOP — ask it to save it as a new Notion page from markdown.

- Weekly digest. Use Hermes’ scheduled jobs to query your project database every Friday and write a short status page for the team.

- Lead capture. Have Hermes add each new enquiry from email or chat to a CRM database, so nothing lives only in someone’s inbox.

- Content calendar. Keep ideas in a Notion database and ask Hermes to draft outlines for anything marked “ready”.

Start with one. Once it runs reliably for a week, add the next. That’s how you build an agent your team actually trusts.

## Safety tips for Hermes and Notion

- Share only what Hermes needs. With the skill, Hermes can only see pages you connect to the integration. Use that to keep private pages private.

- Use separate accounts for work and home. Named connector accounts keep the two apart.

- Know how to switch it off. Setting `tools.connectors.enabled: false` turns connectors off, and `nous.guest: false` turns off the free guest identity.

- Disconnect when you’re done. `hermes connectors disconnect notion` removes access.

For the wider picture of everything Connectors can reach, see my Hermes Agent Connectors guide, and for the full release, my Hermes Agent v0.22 breakdown.

Watch the video below, then follow the steps.

What Hermes Notion actually means

Hermes Agent is the open-source AI agent from Nous Research. On its own it can chat, run commands, browse and remember things. Connecting it to Notion means Hermes can also work inside the place where many teams keep their notes, docs, project trackers and wikis.

Once it’s connected, you can ask Hermes things like “summarise this week’s meeting notes”, “turn this chat into a Notion page” or “add these leads to my CRM database”, and it does the work in Notion for you instead of handing you text to copy and paste.

Since Hermes Agent v0.22.0 (14 October 2026) there are three supported ways to do this. They overlap, so the trick is picking the one that matches how you work:

  • Connectors — the newest and simplest. Hosted apps, a browser sign-in, no keys to copy.
  • The Notion MCP server — Notion’s own hosted MCP endpoint, added from Hermes’ MCP catalog.
  • The bundled notion skill — a skill that teaches Hermes to use the Notion API and Notion’s ntn command-line tool with your own integration key.

Option 1: Connect Notion with Hermes Connectors

Connectors arrived in v0.22. In Nous’ words, they let the agent act in hosted apps such as Linear and Notion through the Nous tool gateway. The flow is short: you ask Hermes for the app, sign in once in your browser, and the Notion tools are usable in the same turn.

You don’t need a Nous account to start. The first time Hermes manages a connection (or you connect from the Desktop app’s Connectors page) it creates a free Nous identity for you. That identity is only used for connectors and managed tools.

There are three places to manage connections:

  • Hermes Desktop: the Connectors page lists hosted apps and MCP servers together. It replaces the old MCP tab.
  • The TUI: type /connectors. The same setup card shows up in the TUI and the CLI.
  • The CLI: hermes connectors list, hermes connectors connect notion, and hermes connectors disconnect notion.

Connectors also support several named accounts per app, which is handy if you keep a work Notion and a personal one. Add a second account with hermes connectors connect notion --alias home. Names can be 1–32 characters using lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. There’s no default account — the tools take a connector_alias, so Hermes always knows which workspace it’s writing to. Reconnecting never deletes anything; the old account is kept as retired, and only you can remove accounts.

One more useful detail: connector tools can send local files as attachments and save the files they return, so Hermes can attach a report it made on your machine to a Notion page.

Option 3: Use the bundled notion skill

Hermes also ships with a notion skill (version 2.0.0, MIT licence) that works on Linux, macOS and Windows. It describes itself as “Notion API + ntn CLI” and covers pages, databases, markdown and Workers.

This route uses your own Notion integration key instead of a hosted sign-in:

  • Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations. The key starts with ntn_ or secret_.
  • Save it as NOTION_API_KEY in ~/.hermes/.env.
  • Share your pages with the integration using the page menu (…) → Connect to. If you skip this, the API returns 404 and Hermes can’t see the page.

On macOS and Linux the skill can also use ntn, Notion’s official CLI. top_items.content:
Hermes Linear turns Hermes Agent into a teammate that can read, sort and create issues in Linear, the project tracker a lot of software and product teams use. Hermes Agent v0.22 makes the connection simple: you can use the new Connectors feature or add Linear’s hosted MCP server from the built-in catalog. Once it’s connected, the useful part starts — triaging new issues, turning chats and scheduled checks into tickets, and writing project updates. This guide covers the setup, then the three Linear workflows I’d use first. Watch the video below, then follow along.

Key takeaways

- Connect with Connectors (sign in once) or the Linear MCP server at `mcp.linear.app/mcp`.

- `hermes mcp configure linear` lets you choose which Linear tools Hermes may call.

- Best uses: issue triage, issues from chats or cron jobs, and project updates.

- Want Hermes running your issue tracker? Claim a free strategy session.

## What Hermes Linear does

Linear is built around issues, projects and cycles. Most of the admin around it is repetitive: reading new bug reports, adding labels, spotting duplicates, chasing status and writing updates. That’s exactly the kind of work an agent is good at.

With Hermes connected to Linear, you can ask in plain English for things like “show me every unassigned bug from this week” or “create an issue for the login error we just talked about”, and Hermes does it in Linear directly.

If you’ve read my Hermes Notion guide, the setup will feel familiar. The difference is the job: Notion is where Hermes writes knowledge; Linear is where Hermes moves work forward.

## Setup option 1: Hermes Connectors

Hermes Agent v0.22.0 added Connectors, which let the agent act in hosted apps such as Linear and Notion through the Nous tool gateway. Ask Hermes to connect Linear, sign in once in your browser, and the Linear tools work in the same turn.

You don’t need an existing Nous account. Your first connection creates a free Nous identity that’s only used for connectors and managed tools. From the terminal, the same thing looks like this:

- `hermes connectors connect linear` — sign in and connect.

- `hermes connectors accounts linear` — see which Linear accounts are connected.

- `hermes connectors connect linear --alias client-a` — add a second named account.

- `hermes connectors disconnect linear` — remove access.

Named accounts matter more for Linear than for most apps. If you work across more than one Linear workspace — say your own company and a client’s — each one gets its own alias, and the tools ask for a `connector_alias`, so issues never land in the wrong workspace.

## Setup option 2: the Linear MCP server

Linear is also in Hermes’ MCP catalog, listed as Linear issue and project management with remote OAuth. The simplest way in is to ask in chat: “add the Linear MCP”. A setup card appears and walks you through it.

If you prefer the terminal, `hermes mcp` opens a picker, `hermes mcp install linear` adds the server and `hermes mcp login linear` runs the sign-in. The config Hermes writes is short:

```
mcp_servers:
  linear:
    url: "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"
    auth: oauth
```

Sign-in uses OAuth 2.1 with a local callback, and the token is stored in `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/` with permissions only you can read.

The real reason to use MCP for Linear is `hermes mcp configure linear`. It opens a checklist of the server’s tools so you can pick what Hermes is allowed to call. In the docs’ example, tools like `find_issues`, `get_issue` and `create_issue` are ticked, while a destructive one like `delete_workspace` is left unticked. That’s the setting I’d care about most before letting an agent loose on a live tracker.

## Workflow 1: Issue triage

Triage is where Hermes earns its keep. New issues come in from customers, support and the team, and someone has to read them, label them and decide who looks at them. Ask Hermes to do the first pass:

- Find new issues that have no labels or assignee.

- Read each one and suggest a label, a priority and a likely owner.

- Flag issues that look like duplicates of existing ones.

- Post a short summary so a human can approve the calls in one go.

Start with Hermes suggesting rather than changing. Once you trust its judgement, let it apply labels directly and keep assignment for a person.

## Workflow 2: Create issues from chats and cron jobs

A lot of good tickets die in chat. Someone mentions a bug in a conversation, everyone agrees it should be fixed, and nobody logs it. With Hermes connected, you can say “make that a Linear issue” and it writes the title, the description and the steps to reproduce from the conversation it just had with you.

The second half is scheduled jobs. Hermes can run tasks on a schedule, which means it can check something regularly and open an issue when it finds a problem. For example: check a list of pages each morning and open an issue if one is down, or review error logs overnight and log anything new. Describe the job to Hermes in plain English and ask it to schedule it; `hermes cron list` shows what’s set up.

## Workflow 3: Project updates

Writing status updates is the job everyone puts off. Hermes can read a project’s issues, see what moved to done, what’s blocked and what’s overdue, and draft the update for you.

Put this on a weekly schedule and you get a consistent Friday update without anyone writing it from scratch. Pair it with my Hermes Notion setup and Hermes can also save that update to a Notion page for people who don’t live in Linear.

Linear is already fast; the slow part is the admin around it. Hermes handles that admin well: first-pass triage, tickets that would otherwise be forgotten, and updates nobody wants to write. Connect it with Connectors, lock down the tools with MCP if you need to, and start with triage. That’s where Hermes Linear pays off first.

top_items.content:
Hermes multiple profiles let you run several separate Hermes agents on one computer — say a coding agent, a research agent and a customer support agent — each with its own settings, memory and bots. With Hermes Agent v0.22, all of those profiles now run through one messaging gateway and one desktop backend, instead of a separate process for each. Create a new profile and its bots go live without a restart. In this guide I explain what a profile is, how the new shared gateway works, what stays separate, and how to set it up. Watch the video below, then follow the steps.

Key takeaways

- A profile is a separate Hermes home: its own config, keys, memory, sessions, skills and cron jobs.

- Since v0.22, one gateway and one desktop backend serve every profile on the machine.

- New profiles go live without a restart; `hermes update` migrates older setups for you.

- Want a multi-agent setup planned for your team? Claim a free strategy session.

## What is a Hermes profile?

According to the Hermes profiles docs, a profile is a separate Hermes home. Each one has its own `config.yaml`, `.env` file with keys, `SOUL.md` personality, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs and database. Profiles live under `~/.hermes/profiles/`.

In plain English: each profile is its own agent. Your coding agent doesn’t share memory with your support agent, and your support bot doesn’t have your personal API keys. That separation is the whole point.

Creating one is a single command: `hermes profile create coder`. Hermes also creates a `coder` command for it, so you can run `coder setup` and `coder chat` straight away.

## What changed in v0.22: one gateway for all profiles

Before Hermes Agent v0.22.0, each profile that talked to Telegram, Discord, Slack and so on needed its own gateway process. Run five profiles and you had five gateways to start, watch and restart.

Now, as the multi-profile gateways guide explains, one messaging gateway and one desktop backend per machine serve every profile. Nous calls this multiplexing, and it’s on by default. When you create a profile, its bots go live without a restart.

Each profile still keeps its own credentials, allowlists, cron jobs and sessions. Only the process is shared. Upgrading is painless too: `hermes update` migrates per-profile setups to the new model automatically.

## What stays separate between profiles

Sharing one process could sound risky, so it’s worth knowing what Hermes keeps apart. The docs list a long table of things each profile resolves from its own files. The ones that matter most:

- Keys and bot tokens come from each profile’s own `.env`. A profile never falls back to the default profile’s keys.

- Who can talk to the bot (allowlists) is set per profile, and closed by default.

- Sessions are stored per profile, so two profiles in the same chat never share history.

- Command approvals are per profile — an “always allow” in one profile doesn’t approve anything in another.

- Logs sit under each profile’s own home.

What’s shared by design is the process itself, its lock and status file, and the one HTTP listener. Webhooks for each profile are served under `/p/<profile>/` on that shared listener.

One rule to remember for chat platforms: each profile needs its own bot token. If two profiles use the same Telegram token, Hermes parks the duplicate and keeps everything else running.

## How to set up multiple Hermes profiles

- Create a profile: `hermes profile create coder`. Add `--description` to label it, or `--clone` to copy settings from your current profile.

- Set it up: `coder setup`, then `coder chat` to talk to it.

- See them all: `hermes profile list`.

- Switch your default: `hermes profile use coder`, and `hermes profile use default` to go back.

- Check the gateway: `hermes gateway status` shows what’s running and explains any refusals.

Cloning is careful by default. Clones skip bot tokens unless you add `--clone-channels`, and profile exports skip your `.ssh`, `.aws` and `.gnupg` folders.

In Hermes Desktop, you can open a profile in its own window or set it as the startup default.

## Managing profiles on the shared gateway

Because there’s now one gateway, the per-profile commands work a little differently:

- `hermes -p coder gateway stop` parks just that profile; `start` or `restart` brings it back. The rest keep running.

- `hermes gateway migrate --multiplex` migrates by hand if you need to, with `--dry-run` to preview first.

- `gateway.standalone: true` in a named profile’s config is a temporary opt-out if one profile must run its own gateway.

- Named profiles refuse `gateway install` and `start` without `--force`, so you don’t accidentally start a second gateway.

Setting `gateway.multiplex_profiles` to false is retired, so the shared gateway is the way forward.

## 3 ways to use multiple profiles

- One agent per job. A coding profile with developer tools, a research profile with web access, and a support profile connected to your customer chat. Each has the right tools and nothing more.

- One agent per client. Agencies can keep each client’s keys, bots and memory in a separate profile, so nothing leaks between accounts.

- Test before production. Try new skills, plugins or models in a test profile before touching the agent your team relies on.

Profiles pair well with delegation. If you want one agent to hand work to others, read my guides to Hermes advanced delegation and choosing a Hermes subagent model.

## Safety notes

Two warnings from the docs are worth repeating. First, never point two agents at the same profile — give each its own. Second, profiles separate settings and data, but they are not a sandbox. A profile running commands on your machine can still reach your files, so set `terminal.cwd` explicitly and use a sandboxed terminal backend for anything risky.

## My verdict on Hermes multiple profiles

Running several agents used to mean juggling several gateways. Now one process serves them all, new profiles go live instantly, and each one still keeps its own keys, bots and memory. If you’ve been cramming every job into one agent, Hermes multiple profiles are the cleaner way to grow into a small team of agents.

top_items.content:
GPT 6.1 Terra vs Sol is the question everyone building with OpenAI is asking this week. OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra as a fast, cheaper model for computer use, visual reasoning and writing, while GPT-6.1 Sol stays its balanced model for hard agentic coding. Terra costs half as much per token. Sol is still the pick for the toughest code. In the video below I walk through Terra, and on this page I put the two side by side so you can choose the right one for each job.

Key takeaways

- Terra costs $1 in / $5 out per million tokens; Sol costs $2 / $10 (OpenAI pricing).

- Terra is built for computer use, visual reasoning and writing, and OpenAI says it finishes tasks over 3x faster than Sol.

- For the most complex coding, OpenAI still recommends Sol (or GPT-6 Astra).

- Not sure which to run? Claim a free strategy session.

Both models come from OpenAI’s GPT-6 family and both take text and images in and give text out. The differences are in price, speed and what each is tuned for. Here are the specs from OpenAI’s own Terra model page, Sol model page and latest-model guide.

## Price: Terra is half the cost

OpenAI says Terra’s standard API prices are 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol (and 50% lower than the older GPT-5.6 Terra). The numbers line up: $1 vs $2 for input and $5 vs $10 for output per million tokens. Cached input is $0.05 on Terra and $0.10 on Sol.

The same pricing rules apply to both: Batch and Flex are 50% cheaper than Standard, and prompts over 272K input tokens cost more. Terra’s Fast mode is 2x Standard. If you run high-volume work — OpenAI’s example is reading invoices and typing the details into accounting software — that halving adds up quickly.

It also matters inside ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI says the same plan allowance covers more tasks with Terra, and substantially more than with GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra.

## Where GPT-6.1 Terra wins

Terra is the screen-and-eyes model. OpenAI built it for the computer-based work that fills a normal day: filling forms, reading technical drawings, editing videos and drafting proposals. These are OpenAI’s own results from the Terra launch post:

- Computer use. On Agents’ Last Exam, Terra at medium effort performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at one-tenth Astra’s price per token, and scores 15 points above GPT-5.6 Terra at about a third of the cost.

- Speed. OpenAI says Terra completes tasks over three times faster than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

- Visual reasoning. On MMMU-Pro, Terra nearly matches GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.

- Desktop apps. On OSWorld 2.1, Terra at medium effort beats GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.

- Fewer mistakes. On OpenAI’s internal set of error-inducing prompts, Terra’s error rate at low effort fell from 53.6% (GPT-5.6 Terra) to 16.7%. At max effort it is 4.3%, which OpenAI says nearly matches Astra and Sol.

- Writing. OpenAI calls out clearer, more natural writing as one of Terra’s strengths.

Terra also supports a `none` reasoning effort, which Sol doesn’t. That’s handy for quick, simple steps where you want an instant answer and no thinking time.

## Where GPT-6.1 Sol wins

OpenAI is direct about this in the Terra post: “For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.” Terra’s coding did improve a lot — it solves 50.3% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 at max effort, more than double GPT-5.6 Terra’s 21.5% — but Sol is the one OpenAI points to for hard code.

Sol’s own numbers back that up. In the GPT-6.1 Sol launch post, OpenAI reports 75.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 at high effort, matching GPT-6 Astra at about a fifth of the cost. In its low-resource languages write-up, OpenAI says Sol migrated COBOL programs with 86.6% success at low effort, rising to 97.9% at higher effort — while noting production work still needs expert review.

There’s one benchmark where OpenAI says Terra comes out ahead. On Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests agents using code for scientific research tasks, Terra at max effort surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost. So for science-style data work, Terra is worth testing before you default to Sol.
